choices.text: Salt is made of NaCl molecules, each one sodium atom joined to one chlorine atom
Salt is a liquid of separate Na+ and Cl- ions that only joins up when it dries
Salt is a giant ionic lattice of sodium and chloride ions, and NaCl gives only the ratio
Salt is made of sodium and chlorine atoms sharing pairs of electrons

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: Table salt is made of NaCl molecules. In fact Salt is a giant ionic lattice: NaCl just gives the ratio, there are no separate NaCl molecules. Each sodium ion is surrounded by chloride ions in one repeating giant structure.
questions.misconception: Table salt is made of NaCl molecules.
questions.prompt: Which statement about table salt is correct?

choices.text: They share a pair of electrons equally between them
Chlorine gives an electron to sodium, forming a chloride ion
Sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine, forming a positive sodium ion and a negative chloride ion
Both atoms keep their electrons and are held by a sea of electrons

questions.explanation: Sodium loses the single electron in its outer shell and chlorine gains it, so both ions end with full outer shells. Losing an electron makes sodium positive; gaining one makes chlorine negative.
questions.prompt: Sodium has electron arrangement 2,8,1 and chlorine has 2,8,7. What happens when they form sodium chloride?

questions.answer: Each chlorine atom contributes one electron to a shared pair between the two atoms. Both atoms count the shared pair in their outer shell, so each has eight outer electrons. No electron is transferred, so no ions form.
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding is sharing, not giving: the shared pair sits between the two nuclei and both atoms count it. Ions only appear when electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
questions.prompt: A chlorine molecule, Cl2, is held together by a covalent bond. Explain, in terms of electrons, how the bond forms and why no ions are made.

questions.answer: Copper is a lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of free-moving electrons. The electrons carry charge through the wire, so it conducts. The layers of ions can slide over each other while the sea still holds them, so the wire bends instead of shattering.
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding pools the outer electrons: they are free to move and carry charge, and sliding ion layers explain malleability - the opposite of the rigid ionic lattice, which shatters when its pattern shifts.
questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of particles and electrons, why copper wire conducts electricity and can be bent without breaking.

choices.text: Melting turns the lattice into NaCl molecules that carry the current
In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice; when molten they are free to move and carry charge
The solid contains no charged particles at all
Heat creates electrons inside the solid that carry the current

questions.explanation: The ions are charged in the solid too, but they cannot move - the lattice holds them in place. Melting frees the ions to move to the electrodes and carry the current. No molecules are involved at any stage.
questions.prompt: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?
